title: Fabrication and Validation of an Organ-on-chip System with Integrated Electrodes to Directly Quantify Transendothelial Electrical Resistance
protocol: Make a PDMS replica of a mold with channel designs using standard photolithography techniques.
Weigh 27 g of PDMS base agent and 2.7 g of curing agent.
Mix the components thoroughly.
Degas the mixture in a desiccator for approximately 45 min.
Prepare the mold by sticking clear tape around it or placing it in a wafer holder.
Pour the degassed PDMS mixture onto the mold.
If air bubbles remain, degas again for approximately 30 min.
Cure the PDMS mixture in an oven at 60 °C for 4 h.
Allow the cured PDMS to cool down.
Pull the cured PDMS from the mold in a cross-flow hood.
Cut the PDMS replica into separate top and bottom chip parts using cutting lines.
Punch four holes in the top parts using a sharp biopsy punch with 1 mm diameter.
Cover the chip parts with clear tape to protect against dust.
Cut polycarbonate membranes from Transwell inserts into squares of approximately 3×3 mm2.
Assemble a porous membrane leakage-free between two PDMS parts to create a two-layer device interfaced with the membrane.
Prepare a PDMS/toluene mortar using 0.7 g of PDMS base agent, 0.07 g of curing agent and 540 µL of toluene at a 5:3 weight ratio.
Vortex the prepared mortar thoroughly.
Spin-coat 200 µL of the mortar onto a glass coverslip at 1500 rpm for 60 s (accelerating at 1000 rpm/s) to obtain a thin, uniform layer.
Transfer a thin layer of the spin-coated mortar from the coverslip onto both a bottom part and a top part of the chip using an ink roller.
Place the bottom part in an oven-safe dish.
Dip the edges of a membrane into the spin-coated mortar and carefully position it in the center of the bottom part.
Carefully place the top part on the bottom part, ensuring proper alignment without applying pressure or sliding to prevent mortar from entering channels.
Cover the chip's inlets with clear tape to protect against dust.
Bake the assembled chips at 60 °C for 3 hours.
Cut platinum wire into pieces of approximately 2 cm.
Clean the cut wire by submerging it in acetone for 30 minutes.
Rinse the cleaned wire with water and ethanol, then allow it to dry.
Put a chip on a plastic dish in a cross-flow hood.
Insert four platinum wires into the electrode channels of the chip using tweezers and bend them down onto the plastic dish.
Insert the wires 0.7-1 mm into the culture channel, past the T-shaped channel junction.
Apply a drop of UV-curable glue at the electrode channel entrance to allow it to fill the channel around the electrode by capillary forces.
Switch on UV light to cure the glue when it reaches the end of the electrode channel.
Fixate the four integrated electrodes to the plastic dish with two-component epoxy adhesive.
Cover the chips with clear tape and bake them at 60 °C for 2 h.
Allow the chips to cool down and store dust-free until use.
Fill both channels with phosphate buffered saline (PBS) to wet them before introducing reagents.
Check under a microscope if there are any air bubbles in the channels.
If air bubbles are present, remove them by flushing with extra PBS.
Fill both channels with 30 μL of 20 μg/mL human fibronectin in PBS.
Incubate at 37 °C for 3 hours.
Check for air bubbles and, if needed, flush the channels with PBS and refill with fibronectin solution.
Flush the chips with endothelial growth medium.
Incubate the chips at 37 °C and 5% CO2 in an incubator for 2 h.
Measure the TEER of the blank chips to ensure that all electrodes are in direct contact with fluid in the channels.
Remove the culture medium from a confluent monolayer of human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells (hCMEC/D3) in a culture flask using PBS.
Add 2 mL of 0.05% trypsin-EDTA and incubate at 37 °C and 5% CO2 for 2-5 minutes until the cells have detached from the culture flask.
Deactivate the trypspin with culture medium supplemented with 20% fetal bovine serum (FBS).
Count the cells and calculate the total number of cells in suspension.
Centrifuge the hCMEC/D3 cells at 390 x g for 5 min and remove supernatant.
Resuspend the cell pellet in endothelial growth medium (EGM-2) to arrive at a concentration of 5 x 106 cells/mL.
Slowly pipette 30 μL of the well-mixed cell suspension into the top channel.
Remove the pipette from the inlet in a fluent motion while still exerting pressure.
Check the seeding density under a microscope.
Incubate the chips at 37 °C and 5% CO2 for at least 1 h.
Flush out any non-attached cells with endothelial culture medium.
Insert culture medium-filled pipette tips as reservoirs in the inlets twice per day.
Replace the medium inside the chip by gravity-driven flow.
Make fluid-fluid contact between the pipette tip and the fluid on top of the chip before inserting the tip into an inlet.
Add a small drop at the in/outlet prior to pipette insertion.
Insert pipette tip reservoirs in the outlets to prevent channels from drying.
Incubate the chips at 37 °C and 5% CO2.
Set up the TEER measurement apparatus consisting of a lock-in amplifier and probe cable circuit.
Take the chip from the incubator and allow it to reach room temperature for at least 10 min.
Remove any fluid from the plastic dish around the electrodes to prevent electrode bridging outside of the chip.
Take the impedance spectrum from 200 Hz to 1 MHz for each combination of two electrodes.
Check if the impedance spectra have expected magnitudes and shapes.
Put the chip back in the incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO2 after finishing measurement.
Process obtained impedance spectra to arrive at a normalized TEER value.
Get the measured resistance between electrodes from the resistive plateau at 10 kHz.
Calculate the TEER using six measured resistances corresponding to one chip.
Subtract the blank TEER from the TEER at all time points to obtain the development of the TEER over time.
